Middleware overview
Control and customize agent execution at every step.
Middleware provides a way to more tightly control what happens inside the agent. Middleware is useful
for:
  Tracking agent behavior with logging, analytics, and debugging.
  Transforming prompts, tool selection, and output formatting.
  Adding retries, fallbacks, and early termination logic.
  Applying rate limits, guardrails, and PII detection.
 Add middleware by passing it to create_agent.
Code: Adding middleware

 Add middleware by passing it to create_agent.
Code: Adding middleware
 from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import SummarizationMiddleware, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
agent = create_agent(
    model="gpt-5.5",
    tools=[...],
    middleware=[
        SummarizationMiddleware(...),
        HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(...)
    ],
)
The agent loop
The core agent loop involves calling a model, letting it choose tools to execute, and then finishing when it
calls no more tools.
Middleware exposes hooks before and after each of those steps.
Use middleware inside a LangGraph workflow
Middleware is not a separate runtime: hooks run inside the compiled LangGraph that create_agent
returns.

Middleware is not a separate runtime: hooks run inside the compiled LangGraph that create_agent
returns.
You can drop the whole agent (middleware and all) into a larger StateGraph as a node or subgraph, and
every middleware hook continues to run.
Reach for this pattern when the surrounding topology is more than a standard "loop until done":
classifying input before routing to one of several agents, fanning out work in parallel, or stitching agent
calls together with deterministic steps.

HumanInTheLoopMiddleware matches against each tool's .name.
@tool-decorated functions take their name from the function, so the key below is "send_email".
Code: Middleware inside a LangGraph workflow
 from langchain.agents import AgentState, create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
from langgraph.graph import START, StateGraph
# Assumes read_email, send_email, classify_node, and route are defined elsewhere.
email_agent = create_agent(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    tools=[read_email, send_email],
    middleware=[HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"send_email": True})],
)
graph = (
    StateGraph(AgentState)
    .add_node("classify", classify_node)
    .add_node("email_agent", email_agent)
    .add_edge(START, "classify")
    .add_conditional_edges("classify", route)
    .compile()
)
What travels with the agent
The HITL interrupt, summarization, PII redaction, retries, and any custom hooks all travel with the agent
node.

The HITL interrupt, summarization, PII redaction, retries, and any custom hooks all travel with the agent
node.
See "Use subgraphs" for the full set of composition patterns, including subgraph checkpointer scoping
(per-invocation versus per-thread).

Legacy Python Application
 Migration Knowledge & System Specification Document
1. Document Purpose
This document describes a legacy Python application that manages users, orders, customer information,
configuration, and report generation. It is intentionally written as an older technical specification so that an
automated code migration agent can analyze the document and identify modernization requirements.
The migration system should retrieve relevant sections when migrating individual modules. Business rules
and observable behavior must be preserved even when the implementation is modernized.

2. Application Overview
The application is a small command-line business management system developed using Python. It
contains a user management module, a local JSON-based persistence layer, an order processing module,
and a configuration module.
The original application was developed using older Python practices. Several parts of the system use
explicit file open and close operations, broad exception handling, manual loops, mutable data structures,
and procedural helper functions.
3. User Management Module
The User component represents a customer of the application. Every user contains a unique identifier, a
name, an email address, and a creation timestamp.
User attributes:

name, an email address, and a creation timestamp.
User attributes:
 user_id — unique customer identifier
 name — customer's display name
 email — customer's email address
 created_at — timestamp indicating when the object was created
The legacy implementation exposes individual getter methods such as get_id(), get_name(), and
get_email(). The print_user() operation writes a formatted user record to the console.
4. User Repository
The UserRepository component provides persistent storage for users. Instead of a relational database, the
legacy application stores user records in a JSON file named users.json.

legacy application stores user records in a JSON file named users.json.
When a new user is saved, the repository checks whether the JSON file exists. If it exists, the existing list
of users is loaded. The new user's information is appended to the list and the complete list is written back
to the file.
The legacy implementation manually opens files and closes them in finally blocks. A migration should
consider replacing this pattern with Python context managers.
The find_user operation searches for a user by identifier. If the JSON file does not exist, the operation

The find_user operation searches for a user by identifier. If the JSON file does not exist, the operation
returns no result. If a matching identifier is found, a User object is reconstructed and returned.

5. User Service
UserService contains application-level operations involving users. It receives a repository object and uses
that repository to retrieve users.
The get_user operation requests a user from the repository. If no user is found, the service prints 'User not
found' and returns no result. If a user exists, the service prints the user information and returns the User
object.
The find_all_users operation receives a collection of user identifiers. It checks each identifier and adds
successfully retrieved users to a result collection. Unknown identifiers are skipped rather than causing the
entire operation to fail.

6. Order Management Module
The Order component represents a customer's purchase. An order contains an order identifier, a customer
identifier, a list of purchased items, and a numeric total.
Order behavior:
 A newly created order has an empty item list.
 The initial total is zero.
 Adding an item appends the item description to the item list.
 The item's price is added to the current total.
 The order can print its identifier, items, and total.
The migration must preserve the total calculation exactly. For example, an order containing items priced at

The migration must preserve the total calculation exactly. For example, an order containing items priced at
2500, 1000, and 500 must have an original total of 4000.
7. Discount Rules
The legacy application calculates discounts using a separate procedural function called
calculate_discount.
Premium customers receive a 20 percent discount. Regular customers receive a 10 percent discount. Any
other customer type receives no discount.
The discount is calculated from the original order total. The final total is calculated by subtracting the
discount from the original total.
8. Order Summary
The generate_order_summary operation creates a dictionary containing the order identifier, customer

discount from the original total.
8. Order Summary
The generate_order_summary operation creates a dictionary containing the order identifier, customer
identifier, items, original total, discount amount, and final total.
The summary is later serialized into a JSON file. The migration may improve the representation of this
data, but the same information must remain available.
9. Configuration Module
The configuration component stores application-wide constants. The legacy system defines the application
name as LegacyMigrationApp, the environment as production, and the maximum retry count as 3.
A print_config operation displays these values. Configuration values should not be accidentally changed
during migration.

A print_config operation displays these values. Configuration values should not be accidentally changed
during migration.
10. Main Application Workflow
The main workflow creates a repository connected to users.json and then creates a UserService using that
repository.
Two users are created and stored: user 101 with the name Alice and user 102 with the name Bob. The
application then searches for users 101, 102, and 999. The unknown user 999 must be ignored.
An order with identifier 5001 is created for customer 101. Three products are added: Keyboard priced at

An order with identifier 5001 is created for customer 101. Three products are added: Keyboard priced at
2500, Mouse priced at 1000, and USB Cable priced at 500. The original order total is therefore 4000.

The customer is treated as a premium customer, so a 20 percent discount is applied. The discount is 800
and the final total is 3200.
The resulting order summary is written to order_summary.json and the application configuration is printed.
11. Legacy Implementation Characteristics
The following characteristics are intentionally present in the legacy design:
1. Explicit file opening and closing.
2. Broad Exception handling in service and persistence code.
3. Manual list construction and indexed loops.
4. Getter methods for simple object attributes.
5. Mutable dictionaries used as data-transfer objects.
6. String concatenation for formatted output.

4. Getter methods for simple object attributes.
5. Mutable dictionaries used as data-transfer objects.
6. String concatenation for formatted output.
7. Procedural functions mixed with object-oriented components.
8. Local JSON files used as a persistence mechanism.
9. Minimal type information.
10. Configuration values stored as class constants.

12. Migration Requirements
The migration agent should modernize the implementation while preserving behavior. Potential
improvements include Python type hints, dataclasses for simple data models, pathlib for filesystem
operations, context managers for file handling, f-strings for formatting, clearer exception handling, and
more readable collection operations.
The agent should not change business rules merely because the implementation is being modernized. In
particular, the premium discount must remain 20 percent, the regular discount must remain 10 percent,
and unknown customer types must receive no discount.

14. Expected Migration Outcome
A successful migration should produce a cleaner, maintainable Python implementation while retaining the
original architecture's core responsibilities and all important business behavior. The migration agent
should be able to retrieve the relevant documentation sections rather than relying only on adjacent text.
This document is intentionally suitable for testing chunking, embedding generation, vector search,
semantic retrieval, and context-aware migration.
